claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia.
source: The Gram-positive bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is the leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia and a major cause of bacteremia and meningitis in children and adults (Loughran et al., 2019; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website, 2019; O'Brien et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Loughran et al., 2019; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website, 2019; O'Brien et al., 2009)

claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major cause of bacteremia and meningitis in children and adults.
source: The Gram-positive bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is the leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia and a major cause of bacteremia and meningitis in children and adults (Loughran et al., 2019; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website, 2019; O'Brien et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Loughran et al., 2019; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website, 2019; O'Brien et al., 2009)

claim: Pneumococcus commonly resides asymptomatically in the nasopharynx.
source: While pneumococcus commonly resides asymptomatically in the nasopharynx, it can cause a wide spectrum of infections in children, elderly, and immunocompromised patients (van der Poll and Opal, 2009; Koedel et al., 2002; Birgitta and Tuomanen, 2013; Bryce et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (van der Poll and Opal, 2009; Koedel et al., 2002; Birgitta and Tuomanen, 2013; Bryce et al., 2005)

claim: Pneumococcus can cause a wide spectrum of infections in children, elderly, and immunocompromised patients.
source: While pneumococcus commonly resides asymptomatically in the nasopharynx, it can cause a wide spectrum of infections in children, elderly, and immunocompromised patients (van der Poll and Opal, 2009; Koedel et al., 2002; Birgitta and Tuomanen, 2013; Bryce et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (van der Poll and Opal, 2009; Koedel et al., 2002; Birgitta and Tuomanen, 2013; Bryce et al., 2005)

claim: Infections by pneumococcus range from non-invasive diseases such as otitis media and sinusitis to life-threatening bacteremia and meningitis.
source: Infections by pneumococcus range from non-invasive diseases, such as otitis media and sinusitis to life-threatening bacteremia and meningitis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the spectrum of pneumococcal disease

claim: The polysaccharide capsule is considered the most important virulence factor of S. pneumoniae.
source: Currently available vaccines target the polysaccharide capsule (CPS), which is considered the most important virulence factor of S. pneumoniae.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about pneumococcal virulence

claim: There are more than 90 different capsular serotypes of S. pneumoniae.
source: Although there are more than 90 different capsular serotypes (Bentley et al., 2006), the current vaccines only include a limited number of serotypes including those most frequently found to be causing invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Bentley et al., 2006)

claim: Current vaccines only include a limited number of serotypes including those most frequently found to be causing invasive pneumococcal disease.
source: Although there are more than 90 different capsular serotypes (Bentley et al., 2006), the current vaccines only include a limited number of serotypes including those most frequently found to be causing invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD).
evidence: This is established knowledge about current pneumococcal vaccine composition

claim: Widespread vaccination has been highly effective in lowering invasive pneumococcal disease caused by vaccine serotypes.
source: Besides the fact that the widespread vaccination has been highly effective in lowering IPD caused by vaccine serotypes (Scott et al., 2009; Whitney et al., 2003; Shinefield and Black, 2000), there still is a large burden of pneumococcal disease caused by non-vaccine serotypes.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Scott et al., 2009; Whitney et al., 2003; Shinefield and Black, 2000)

claim: There is still a large burden of pneumococcal disease caused by non-vaccine serotypes.
source: Besides the fact that the widespread vaccination has been highly effective in lowering IPD caused by vaccine serotypes (Scott et al., 2009; Whitney et al., 2003; Shinefield and Black, 2000), there still is a large burden of pneumococcal disease caused by non-vaccine serotypes.
evidence: This is an inference from the effectiveness of vaccines against vaccine serotypes but continued disease burden

claim: Some vaccine serotypes induce a weak immune response making it difficult to control pneumococcal disease, particularly in risk groups.
source: Furthermore, because some vaccine serotypes induce a weak immune response it remains difficult to control pneumococcal disease, particularly in risk groups (Pirofski and Casadevall, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Pirofski and Casadevall, 1998)

claim: The emergence of strains with high level of antibiotic resistance highlights a strong need to develop new therapeutic strategies against pneumococcal infections.
source: Finally, the emergence of strains with high level of antibiotic resistance (Mclntyre, 1997; Aguinagalde et al., 2015; Greenwood, 1999; Novak et al., 1999) highlights a strong need to develop new therapeutic strategies against pneumococcal infections.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Mclntyre, 1997; Aguinagalde et al., 2015; Greenwood, 1999; Novak et al., 1999) and logical inference about the need for alternatives

claim: Antibody therapies have emerged as a successful treatment for several autoimmune diseases and cancers in recent years.
source: In recent years, antibody therapies have emerged as a successful treatment for several autoimmune diseases and cancers (Scott et al., 2012; Edwards et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Scott et al., 2012; Edwards et al., 2004)

claim: Human immune protection against pneumococci critically depends on the action of the human complement system.
source: As evidenced by recurrent infections in patients with genetic complement deficiencies (Ram et al., 2010; Carneiro-Sampaio and Coutinho, 2007), human immune protection against pneumococci critically depends on the action of the human complement system (Kaufmann and Dorhoi, 2016; Bardoel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Ram et al., 2010; Carneiro-Sampaio and Coutinho, 2007; Kaufmann and Dorhoi, 2016; Bardoel et al., 2014)

claim: Patients with genetic complement deficiencies experience recurrent infections.
source: As evidenced by recurrent infections in patients with genetic complement deficiencies (Ram et al., 2010; Carneiro-Sampaio and Coutinho, 2007), human immune protection against pneumococci critically depends on the action of the human complement system (Kaufmann and Dorhoi, 2016; Bardoel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Ram et al., 2010; Carneiro-Sampaio and Coutinho, 2007)

claim: Complement proteins circulate as inactive precursors but become rapidly activated upon contact with bacterial cells.
source: These proteins circulate as inactive precursors but become rapidly activated upon contact with bacterial cells (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Wang et al., 2016)

claim: An activated complement cascade triggers labeling of bacteria with C3-derived opsonins (C3b and iC3b) that potently induce phagocytosis and subsequent intracellular killing of bacteria by professional phagocytes.
source: An activated complement cascade triggers a variety of immune responses, such as the labeling of bacteria with C3-derived opsonins (C3b and iC3b) that potently induce phagocytosis and subsequent intracellular killing of bacteria by professional phagocytes (opsonophagocytic killing) (Dunkelberger and Song, 2010; Stuart and Ezekowitz, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Dunkelberger and Song, 2010; Stuart and Ezekowitz, 2005)

claim: Complement is essential in immune protection against S. pneumoniae.
source: Because complement is essential in immune protection against S. pneumoniae (Kadioglu et al., 2008; Standish and Weiser, 2009), the capacity of antibodies to induce complement activation could be exploited for effective antibacterial therapies.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kadioglu et al., 2008; Standish and Weiser, 2009)

claim: The capsule is believed to block immune activation by shielding epitopes and blocking deposition of C3 opsonins.
source: This is especially unclear for encapsulated S. pneumoniae strains because the capsule is believed to block immune activation, for instance, by shielding epitopes and blocking deposition of C3 opsonins (Hyams et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Hyams et al., 2010)

claim: Target-bound IgGs should organize into higher-order oligomers (IgG hexamers) to provide an optimal docking platform for complement component C1q.
source: Furthermore, recent studies showed that target-bound IgGs should organize into higher-order oligomers (IgG hexamers) to provide an optimal docking platform for complement component C1q (Diebolder et al., 2014; de Jong et al., 2016; Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Diebolder et al., 2014; de Jong et al., 2016) and illustrated in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Each antibody-binding headpiece of C1q has a low affinity for IgG.
source: Because each antibody-binding headpiece of C1q has a low affinity for IgG, physiological binding occurs when the six headpieces simultaneously bind to IgG once hexamerized.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C1q-IgG interactions

claim: Physiological binding of C1q occurs when the six headpieces simultaneously bind to IgG once hexamerized.
source: Because each antibody-binding headpiece of C1q has a low affinity for IgG, physiological binding occurs when the six headpieces simultaneously bind to IgG once hexamerized.
evidence: This is an inference from the low affinity of individual C1q headpieces for IgG

claim: Anti-capsular antibodies as wild-type IgG have a poor capacity to form IgG hexamers and trigger downstream opsonophagocytic killing via complement.
source: Our data suggest that these anti-capsular antibodies as wild-type IgG have a poor capacity to form IgG hexamers and trigger downstream opsonophagocytic killing via complement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The limitation of poor hexamer formation can be overcome by the introduction of a single amino acid mutation that enhances hexamerization of anti-capsular antibodies and strongly potentiates complement-mediated opsonophagocytic killing of pneumococci, both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Importantly, this limitation can be overcome by the introduction of a single amino acid mutation that enhances hexamerization of anti-capsular antibodies and strongly potentiates complement-mediated opsonophagocytic killing of pneumococci, both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Serotype 6B is a common serotype infecting both adults and children.
source: To study whether human mAbs can induce complement activation on encapsulated S. pneumoniae strains, we first investigated complement activation on S. pneumoniae 6B, a common serotype infecting both adults and children (Luján et al., 2010; Siber, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Luján et al., 2010; Siber, 1994)

claim: Serotype 6B is covered by current vaccines.
source: Although serotype 6B is covered by current vaccines, the 6B capsule type is found to be poorly immunogenic and an important risk factor in the mortality by IPD (Luján et al., 2010; Siber, 1994; Sun et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about vaccine coverage

claim: The 6B capsule type is found to be poorly immunogenic and an important risk factor in the mortality by invasive pneumococcal disease.
source: Although serotype 6B is covered by current vaccines, the 6B capsule type is found to be poorly immunogenic and an important risk factor in the mortality by IPD (Luján et al., 2010; Siber, 1994; Sun et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Luján et al., 2010; Siber, 1994; Sun et al., 1999)

claim: A human IgG1 antibody recognizes a carbohydrate structure α-D-Glcp(1→3)α-L-Rhap present on serogroup 6 strains.
source: We generated recombinant variants of a previously identified human IgG1 antibody that recognizes a carbohydrate structure present on serogroup 6 strains: α-D-Glcp(1→3)α-L-Rhap (Park et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Park et al., 2009)

claim: Single amino acid mutations E430G or E345K were introduced to enhance Fc-dependent hexamerization of target-bound antibodies.
source: Specifically, mutations E430G (Glu430 → Gly) or E345K (Glu345 →Lys) were introduced because of their proven strong enhancement of complement-dependent lysis of tumor cells while retaining properties required for the development of biopharmaceuticals (Diebolder et al., 2014; de Jong et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Diebolder et al., 2014; de Jong et al., 2016)

claim: Mutations E430G and E345K have proven strong enhancement of complement-dependent lysis of tumor cells while retaining properties required for the development of biopharmaceuticals.
source: Specifically, mutations E430G (Glu430 → Gly) or E345K (Glu345 →Lys) were introduced because of their proven strong enhancement of complement-dependent lysis of tumor cells while retaining properties required for the development of biopharmaceuticals (Diebolder et al., 2014; de Jong et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Diebolder et al., 2014; de Jong et al., 2016)

claim: The introduction of hexamer-enhancing mutations did not affect the binding of CPS6-IgG1 antibodies to serotype 6B.
source: After verifying that the introduction of hexamer-enhancing mutations did not affect the binding of CPS6-IgG1 antibodies to serotype 6B (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3), we studied their capacity to induce complement activation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3

claim: Introduction of hexamer-enhancing mutations in CPS6-IgG1 allowed activation of the classical complement pathway.
source: Importantly, we found that introduction of hexamer-enhancing mutations in CPS6-IgG1 allowed activation of the classical complement pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on C1q recruitment and downstream complement activation

claim: Recruitment of C1q to target-bound IgGs induces activation of C1q-attached C1r and C1s proteases that cleave C4 to covalently attach activated C4b molecules onto the bacterial surface.
source: Recruitment of C1q to target-bound IgGs induces activation of C1q-attached C1r and C1s proteases that cleave C4 to covalently attach activated C4b molecules onto the bacterial surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Müller-Eberhard et al., 1967).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Müller-Eberhard et al., 1967) and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: C1 activates C2 to produce a C3 convertase (C4b2b) that deposits large amounts of C3b.
source: Furthermore, C1 activates C2 to produce a C3 convertase (C4b2b) that deposits large amounts of C3b, a key component of the complement cascade that labels bacteria for phagocytosis (Brown et al., 1983; Joiner et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Brown et al., 1983; Joiner et al., 1984)

claim: C3b is a key component of the complement cascade that labels bacteria for phagocytosis.
source: Furthermore, C1 activates C2 to produce a C3 convertase (C4b2b) that deposits large amounts of C3b, a key component of the complement cascade that labels bacteria for phagocytosis (Brown et al., 1983; Joiner et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Brown et al., 1983; Joiner et al., 1984)

claim: Fc-engineered variants of CPS6-IgG1, but not the WT antibody, potently induced deposition of C4b onto serotype 6B.
source: Indeed, by monitoring deposition of C4b and C3b molecules, we observed that Fc-engineered variants of CPS6-IgG1, but not the WT antibody, potently induced deposition of C4b (Figure 1e) and C3b molecules (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 4) onto serotype 6B.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e

claim: Fc-engineered variants of CPS6-IgG1, but not the WT antibody, potently induced deposition of C3b molecules onto serotype 6B.
source: Indeed, by monitoring deposition of C4b and C3b molecules, we observed that Fc-engineered variants of CPS6-IgG1, but not the WT antibody, potently induced deposition of C4b (Figure 1e) and C3b molecules (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 4) onto serotype 6B.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: Hexamer-enhancing mutations can overcome poor complement activation by monoclonal antibodies against capsular serotype 6.
source: Altogether, these data show that hexamer-enhancing mutations can overcome poor complement activation by monoclonal antibodies against capsular serotype 6.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on complement activation

claim: Neutrophils are crucial to establish immune protection against pneumococcal infections.
source: Neutrophils are crucial to establish immune protection against pneumococcal infections (Ullah et al., 2017; Lewis and Surewaard, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Ullah et al., 2017; Lewis and Surewaard, 2018)

claim: Neutrophils are the first to be recruited from the blood to the site of infection where they engulf and internalize bacteria via phagocytosis.
source: These cells are the first to be recruited from the blood to the site of infection where they engulf and internalize bacteria via phagocytosis to, subsequently, kill them by exposure to antimicrobial agents such as antimicrobial peptides, reactive oxygen species, and enzymes (Bardoel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Bardoel et al., 2014)

claim: Neutrophils kill bacteria by exposure to antimicrobial agents such as antimicrobial peptides, reactive oxygen species, and enzymes.
source: These cells are the first to be recruited from the blood to the site of infection where they engulf and internalize bacteria via phagocytosis to, subsequently, kill them by exposure to antimicrobial agents such as antimicrobial peptides, reactive oxygen species, and enzymes (Bardoel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Bardoel et al., 2014)

claim: The phagocytic uptake is greatly enhanced by the tagging of bacteria with IgG antibodies that can engage Fcγ receptors.
source: The phagocytic uptake is greatly enhanced by the tagging of bacteria with IgG antibodies that can engage Fcγ receptors (FcγRs) (Nimmerjahn and Ravetch, 2006) and/or C3-derived opsonins that can mediate the uptake of bacteria via complement receptors (Stuart and Ezekowitz, 2005; van Lookeren Campagne et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Nimmerjahn and Ravetch, 2006)

claim: C3-derived opsonins can mediate the uptake of bacteria via complement receptors.
source: The phagocytic uptake is greatly enhanced by the tagging of bacteria with IgG antibodies that can engage Fcγ receptors (FcγRs) (Nimmerjahn and Ravetch, 2006) and/or C3-derived opsonins that can mediate the uptake of bacteria via complement receptors (Stuart and Ezekowitz, 2005; van Lookeren Campagne et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Stuart and Ezekowitz, 2005; van Lookeren Campagne et al., 2007)

claim: The CPS6-IgG1-WT antibody poorly induced phagocytosis of serotype 6B.
source: First, we observed that the CPS6-IgG1-WT antibody poorly induced phagocytosis of serotype 6B (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: Hexamer-enhanced variants of CPS6-IgG1 induced very potent phagocytosis.
source: In contrast, hexamer-enhanced variants of CPS6-IgG1 induced very potent phagocytosis (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: For both E430G and E345K mutated variants, 0.3 μg/ml of mAb induced maximum phagocytosis in the presence of 2.5% IgG/M-depleted serum.
source: For both E430G and E345K mutated variants, we found that 0.3 μg/ml of mAb induced maximum phagocytosis in the presence of 2.5% IgG/M-depleted serum (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a

claim: When serum was heat-treated to inactivate complement, phagocytosis by E430G and E345K antibodies was completely abolished.
source: When serum was heat-treated to inactivate complement (Berends et al., 2015), we found that phagocytosis by E430G and E345K antibodies was completely abolished (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and citation to published literature (Berends et al., 2015)

claim: Opsonization with both E430G and E345K antibodies in the presence of active complement resulted in bacterial internalization.
source: Opsonization with both E430G and E345K antibodies in the presence of active complement clearly resulted in bacterial internalization (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Opsonization by WT antibody resulted in mainly free extracellular localized bacteria.
source: In contrast, opsonization by WT antibody resulted in mainly free extracellular localized bacteria (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Phagocytic uptake via hexamerization-enhanced CPS6 antibodies is fully depended on the presence of complement.
source: This indicates that phagocytic uptake via hexamerization-enhanced CPS6 antibodies is fully depended on the presence of complement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing abolished phagocytosis with heat-inactivated serum

claim: Fc-III is a cyclic peptide that binds to IgG residues involved in the Fc-Fc interaction interface.
source: To study whether phagocytosis via hexamer-enhanced antibodies indeed depends on Fc-dependent IgG oligomerization, we analyzed phagocytosis in the presence of Fc-III, a cyclic peptide that binds to IgG residues involved in the Fc-Fc interaction interface (DeLano et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (DeLano et al., 2000)

claim: IgG-RGY (combination of E345R, E430G, and S440Y mutations) has the capacity to form stable hexamers in solution.
source: To study this end, we combined native mass spectrometry (Leney and Heck, 2017; Tamara et al., 2022) with an IgG triple mutant (IgG-RGY, combination of E345R (Glu345 → Arg), E430G (Glu430 → Gly), and S440Y (Ser440 → Tyr) mutations) that has the capacity to form stable hexamers in solution (Diebolder et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Leney and Heck, 2017; Tamara et al., 2022; Diebolder et al., 2014)

claim: Native mass spectra of IgG1-RGY revealed the presence of monomeric and hexameric species, with intermediate states observed at lower abundance.
source: In agreement with prior work, native mass spectra of IgG1-RGY revealed the presence of monomeric and hexameric species, with intermediate states observed at lower abundance (Figure 2e; Wang et al., 2016; Diebolder et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e and citations to published literature (Wang et al., 2016; Diebolder et al., 2014)

claim: When IgG1-RGY was incubated with Fc-III, the relative abundance of IgG oligomers was diminished.
source: When IgG1-RGY was incubated with Fc-III, however, the relative abundance of IgG oligomers was diminished.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e

claim: A scrambled version of Fc-III (Scr) does not bind IgG1 molecules.
source: No effect was observed for a scrambled version of the same peptide (Scr) that in contrast to Fc-III does not bind IgG1 molecules (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Fc-III inhibits IgG-mediated complement activation by competitive binding to the Fc-Fc interaction interface of IgG monomers.
source: The fact that we observed binding of Fc-III to monomeric IgG1, but not to larger oligomeric species, suggests that Fc-III inhibits IgG-mediated complement activation by competitive binding to the Fc-Fc interaction interface of IgG monomers.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that Fc-III binds to monomeric IgG1 but not to oligomers

claim: Fc-III potently blocked phagocytic uptake of serotype 6B via both E430G and E345K mutants, while Scr showed no effect.
source: In line with our hypothesis, we found that Fc-III potently blocked phagocytic uptake of serotype 6B via both E430G and E345K mutants, while Scr showed no effect (Figure 2f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f

claim: IgM antibodies already pre-exist as pentameric or hexameric oligomers that are kept together via covalent bonds.
source: Finally, considering that IgM antibodies already pre-exist as pentameric or hexameric oligomers that are kept together via covalent bonds, we compared the capacity of anti-CPS6-IgM to induce pneumococcal complement-mediated phagocytosis with our hexamerization-enhancing variants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IgM structure

claim: IgM does induce complement-dependent phagocytosis of pneumococcal serotype 6B, but it was less potent than CPS6-IgG1-E430G and E345K variants.
source: Although IgM does induce complement-dependent phagocytosis of pneumococcal serotype 6B, it was less potent than CPS6-IgG1-E430G and E345K variants (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g and Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: Complement activation via pre-assembled IgM oligomers was less effective than via IgG hexamers that are formed after target binding.
source: This suggests that complement activation via pre-assembled IgM oligomers was less effective than via IgG hexamers that are formed after target binding.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that IgM was less potent than hexamer-enhanced IgG variants

claim: While a WT monoclonal IgG antibody against CPS6 has a poor capacity to induce phagocytosis of S. pneumoniae serotype 6B, introduction of hexamerization-enhancing mutations strongly increases complement-mediated phagocytosis.
source: Taken together, while a WT monoclonal IgG antibody against CPS6 has a poor capacity to induce phagocytosis of S. pneumoniae serotype 6B, introduction of hexamerization-enhancing mutations strongly increases complement-mediated phagocytosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on phagocytosis

claim: The natural antibody response against bacterial capsule polysaccharides is dominated by IgG2.
source: Because the natural antibody response against bacterial capsule polysaccharides is dominated by IgG2 (Siber et al., 1980; Ferrante et al., 1990; Schauer et al., 2003), we also constructed human monoclonal CPS6-IgG2.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Siber et al., 1980; Ferrante et al., 1990; Schauer et al., 2003)

claim: CPS6-IgG2-WT and Fc-Fc-enhancing variants showed equal binding to serotype 6B.
source: While CPS6-IgG2-WT and Fc-Fc-enhancing variants showed equal binding to serotype 6B (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), we again observed that hexamer-enhancing mutations E430G and E345K both improved C3b deposition in IgG2 (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a

claim: Hexamer-enhancing mutations E430G and E345K both improved C3b deposition in IgG2.
source: While CPS6-IgG2-WT and Fc-Fc-enhancing variants showed equal binding to serotype 6B (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), we again observed that hexamer-enhancing mutations E430G and E345K both improved C3b deposition in IgG2 (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a

claim: For IgG3 antibodies, hexamer-enhancing mutation E345K significantly increased C3b deposition, while a much less strong enhancement was observed for E430G.
source: Also for IgG3 antibodies, which are considered more effective in the induction of Fc-effector functions (Vidarsson et al., 2014), we found that the mutants had equal binding and hexamer-enhancing mutation E345K significantly increased C3b deposition, while a much less strong enhancement was observed for E430G (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b

claim: IgG3 antibodies are considered more effective in the induction of Fc-effector functions.
source: Also for IgG3 antibodies, which are considered more effective in the induction of Fc-effector functions (Vidarsson et al., 2014), we found that the mutants had equal binding and hexamer-enhancing mutation E345K significantly increased C3b deposition, while a much less strong enhancement was observed for E430G (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Vidarsson et al., 2014)

claim: CPS6-IgG1-E345K activated complement more potently than CPS6-IgG3-E345K and CPS6-IgG2-E345K.
source: A direct comparison of E345K variants shows that CPS6-IgG1-E345K activated complement more potently than CPS6-IgG3-E345K and CPS6-IgG2-E345K (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e), even though the binding is the same (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e, 1c, and 1d

claim: E345K, but not E430G, enhanced phagocytosis of CPS6-IgG3.
source: Consistent with the results for C3b deposition, we observed that E345K, but not E430G, enhanced phagocytosis of CPS6-IgG3 (Figure 3d) while a very moderate effect was observed for IgG2 (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d

claim: A very moderate effect on phagocytosis was observed for IgG2.
source: Consistent with the results for C3b deposition, we observed that E345K, but not E430G, enhanced phagocytosis of CPS6-IgG3 (Figure 3d) while a very moderate effect was observed for IgG2 (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c

claim: Phagocytosis of CPS6-IgG3 fully relied on the presence of active complement.
source: Again, phagocytosis of CPS6-IgG3 fully relied on the presence of active complement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1f

claim: The α-D-Glcp(1→3)α-L-Rhap antigen is found in the CPS of serotypes 6A, 6C, and 19A but not in the 19F CPS.
source: Next to serotype 6B, the α-D-Glcp(1→3)α-L-Rhap antigen is also found in the CPS of serotypes 6A, 6C, and 19A but not in the 19F CPS (Park et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Park et al., 2009)

claim: Serotype 19A is a highly invasive serotype that, despite coverage in PCV-13 vaccine, remains one of the most frequently carried pneumococcal serotypes in children, and major cause of disease in European countries and the United States.
source: Serotype 19A is of particular interest because this is a highly invasive serotype that, despite coverage in PCV-13 vaccine, remains one of the most frequently carried pneumococcal serotypes in children, and major cause of disease in European countries and the United States (Kaplan et al., 2010; Isturiz et al., 2017; Bosch et al., 2016; Richter et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kaplan et al., 2010; Isturiz et al., 2017; Bosch et al., 2016; Richter et al., 2013)

claim: There is a significant increase in penicillin and multidrug resistance among 19A clinical isolates.
source: Furthermore, there is a significant increase in penicillin and multidrug resistance among 19A clinical isolates (Richter et al., 2009; Beall et al., 2011; Ardanuy et al., 2009; Muñoz-Almagro et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Richter et al., 2009; Beall et al., 2011; Ardanuy et al., 2009; Muñoz-Almagro et al., 2009)

claim: Hexamer-enhancing variants of CPS6-IgG1 bind to serotype 19A but not to 19F.
source: After validating that (hexamer-enhancing variants of) CPS6-IgG1 indeed bind to serotype 19A but not to 19F (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and d), we tested complement activation and phagocytosis of this strain.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and d

claim: Hexamer-enhancing mutations strongly increased complement activation on serotype 19A, as evidenced by increased detection of C1q, C4b, and C3b, especially when E345K mutation was present.
